To date, only minimal human testing has been published. A recent pilot study in 2025 administered BPC-157 intravenously to two healthy adult volunteers to assess safety. The participants received 10 mg on the first day and 20 mg on the second day by slow infusion. The results were encouraging in terms of safety: no adverse effects were observed, and detailed blood tests showed no harmful changes in liver, kidney, heart, or metabolic function after the infusions.

While this finding supports the idea that BPC-157 may be safe in the short term, the sample size was only two people – far too small to draw broad conclusions. More rigorous safety trials with larger participant groups are needed to confirm safety in humans.
In the absence of official trials, some healthcare practitioners (particularly in sports medicine or integrative medicine) have experimented with BPC-157 as an off-label therapy. For example:

A physician-authored report described 12 patients with knee injuries or osteoarthritis who received BPC-157 injections into the knee joint, with 11 of 12 reporting improvements. However, this was not a controlled study with no placebo group, and outcomes were based on patient self-reports.

A small pilot trial at a private clinic treated women suffering from chronic bladder pain by injecting BPC-157 into the bladder wall, noting symptom relief and no immediate side effects. This too lacked a control group and was an open-label observation.

Such reports must be viewed cautiously, as they are not the gold standard evidence required for medical approval. They do, however, suggest interest in exploring BPC-157's potential despite the unknowns.

A formal Phase I clinical trial (code-named PCO-02) was conducted around 2015 on 42 healthy volunteers to evaluate BPC-157's pharmacokinetics and safety. However, the results of that trial were never published. The trial was completed, but the data were not reported, which has raised questions in the research community. Without publication, the findings remain unknown.

Human experience with BPC-157 remains in early, experimental stages. Small studies and individual experiments hint at effects consistent with animal research, but robust clinical evidence to verify efficacy or proper protocols is lacking. Experts consistently stress that BPC-157 should not be used in routine medical practice yet. It remains a compound with potential, but until large controlled trials are conducted, any human use is effectively experimental.

To date, only minimal human testing has been published. A 2025 pilot study (Lee and Burgess, Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine; PMID 40131143), carried out at a private clinic in Florida, gave BPC-157 by intravenous infusion on two consecutive days to two adults who had received intravenous BPC-157 before. The authors reported no side effects and no measurable changes in the tested heart, liver, kidney, thyroid and blood glucose markers.

With two participants, no control group and three days of follow-up, the study cannot establish safety. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee notes that the published human studies of BPC-157 were of short duration, had small sample sizes and gave limited information on safety.

entries.value: A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, PCO-02 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02637284, sponsor PharmaCotherapia), was registered in December 2015 to assess the safety and pharmacokinetics of BPC-157 oral tablets against placebo, with a single-administration part and a two-week repeated-administration part and an estimated enrollment of 42. The registry record was last updated in December 2015, its status is listed as unknown, and no results are posted. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA was unable to find an associated published study.

In dogs, daily injections for a month at doses up to 1 mg/kg showed no significant adverse effects compared to control animals
Studies reported no changes in body weight, behavior, or organ health attributable to BPC-157

target_values.title: Animal Toxicology Data

entries.value: Published animal toxicology data on BPC-157 are limited. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee summarizes one published set of studies (Xu et al. 2020, Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology; PMID 32334036; by a group developing BPC-157 as a drug, developer-affiliated) in which rats and dogs were given BPC-157 (free base) by intramuscular injection:
Single-administration study in rats and dogs: the authors reported no signs of acute toxicity and no histopathological changes in various organs 14 days after treatment.

28-day studies in rats and dogs (once-daily treatment at three levels, saline-treated controls, 14-day recovery period): the authors reported no significant effects on body weight, behavior, survival or organ histopathology, but FDA notes that the histopathological data are not included in the article. FDA’s reading is that the 28-day treatment appeared to be associated with clinically relevant safety signals, including altered clotting measures (aPTT) and liver-associated signals (increased serum ALT, glucose and triglyceride levels).

Gaps identified by FDA: no carcinogenicity studies, no longer-term repeated-treatment studies, and no toxicity or pharmacokinetic studies by the oral, rectal, subcutaneous or nasal routes nominated for compounding. FDA states that intramuscular results cannot be used to estimate no-adverse-effect levels for those other routes.

target_values.title: Theoretical Concerns

entries.value: Animal and cell studies have reported that BPC-157 may increase growth-factor signalling and blood-vessel formation (angiogenesis). Because tumours also use these pathways, some researchers have raised a theoretical question about effects on existing cancers. This has not been tested: FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA did not identify any carcinogenicity studies of BPC-157 (free base) or BPC-157 acetate. The cancer risk is therefore unknown, not ruled out.

As of 19 October 2026, BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23), and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published. FDA has also found some clinics compounding it. See "U.S. regulatory status — compounding review" below for the July 2026 advisory committee meeting and the October 2026 interim policy submitted for OIRA review.

Products sold as "research chemicals" are not FDA-regulated drugs. Many websites sell BPC-157 with disclaimers that it is not for human use. This grey market means quality control is questionable: products might not contain the stated amount or could have impurities.

target_values.title: U.S. regulatory status — compounding review (as of 19 October 2026)

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published as of 19 October 2026. In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and compounding: an advisory committee vote in July and an interim policy sent for White House review in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or makes it lawful to compound.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) met on 23–24 July 2026. On 23 July it considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the list of bulk drug substances that may be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the "503A Bulks List"). FDA evaluated both forms for ulcerative colitis. FDA's published voting questions were: "Should BPC-157 (free base) be placed on the list?" and "Should BPC-157 acetate be placed on the list?" In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither BPC-157 (free base) nor BPC-157 acetate be included on the 503A Bulks List. FDA states that advisory committee recommendations are non-binding. Reuters reported on 15 October 2026 that the advisers had recommended FDA loosen restrictions on six of the seven peptides reviewed in July, including BPC-157. As of 19 October 2026, FDA has not posted official minutes or vote tallies on the meeting page, so this entry gives no vote counts. The 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23) has not been amended to include BPC-157.

Interim access policy under OIRA review (received 14 October 2026). OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) lists a pending Executive Order 12866 review with these details (reginfo.gov, checked 19 October 2026; status "Pending EO 12866 Regulatory Review"). Title: "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides". Agency/Subagency: HHS / FDA. RIN: 0910-ZD94. Stage: Notice. Received Date: 10/14/2026. Legal Deadline: None. Economically Significant: No. The listing does not name any peptides and does not include the policy text. As of 19 October 2026, no matching Federal Register document and no FDA press announcement were found. Reuters, citing an Associated Press report based on two unnamed people, reported that the policy would allow some popular peptides, including BPC-157, to be compounded. That is a press report and has not been confirmed in any published text. Reginfo.gov lists three EO 12866 meetings on this review, on 21, 23 and 27 October 2026 (checked 22 October 2026); the 21 October meeting was requested by the American Academy of Peptide Medicine. EO 12866 meetings let outside parties present their views to OIRA while a review is pending; a scheduled meeting is not a decision and does not indicate the outcome.
Not an approval: neither the PCAC vote nor the OIRA submission is FDA approval of BPC-157 for any use.
No published text: the policy text has not been released, and no Federal Register notice has been located.
No effective or start date: none has been announced.
Scope unknown: the OIRA listing does not say which peptides would be covered.
Review is not a final policy: an OIRA review is a step before publication. The policy may be changed, withdrawn, or published in a different form.

Other status lines are unchanged: on FDA's "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" page (content current as of 22 April 2026), BPC-157 is listed as nominated but withdrawn. BPC-157 remains on WADA's S0 (non-approved substances) list.

target_values.title: World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)

entries.value: WADA has banned BPC-157 for athletes under the class of "S0: Non-approved substances." This means athletes can face sanctions if caught using it in sport. The ban signals that BPC-157 is considered experimental and not recognized as a legitimate medication.

target_values.title: Animal Toxicology Data

entries.value: Published animal toxicology data on BPC-157 are limited. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee summarizes one published set of studies (Xu et al. 2020, Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology; PMID 32334036; by a group developing BPC-157 as a drug, developer-affiliated) in which rats and dogs were given BPC-157 (free base) by intramuscular injection:
Single-administration study in rats and dogs: the authors reported no signs of acute toxicity and no histopathological changes in various organs 14 days after treatment.

28-day studies in rats and dogs (once-daily treatment at three levels, saline-treated controls, 14-day recovery period): the authors reported no significant effects on body weight, behavior, survival or organ histopathology, but FDA notes that the histopathological data are not included in the article. FDA’s reading is that the 28-day treatment appeared to be associated with clinically relevant safety signals, including altered clotting measures (aPTT) and liver-associated signals (increased serum ALT, glucose and triglyceride levels).

Gaps identified by FDA: no carcinogenicity studies, no longer-term repeated-treatment studies, and no toxicity or pharmacokinetic studies by the oral, rectal, subcutaneous or nasal routes nominated for compounding. FDA states that intramuscular results cannot be used to estimate no-adverse-effect levels for those other routes.

target_values.title: Theoretical Concerns

entries.value: Animal and cell studies have reported that BPC-157 may increase growth-factor signalling and blood-vessel formation (angiogenesis). Because tumours also use these pathways, some researchers have raised a theoretical question about effects on existing cancers. This has not been tested: FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA did not identify any carcinogenicity studies of BPC-157 (free base) or BPC-157 acetate. The cancer risk is therefore unknown, not ruled out.

The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

findings.title: Wound and Muscle Healing
findings.content: Animal studies demonstrate accelerated healing of skin incisions and muscle tears when BPC-157 is applied. In rats with partially torn or crushed muscles, treated animals showed quicker healing and more complete muscle fiber regeneration compared to untreated controls in various research summaries.

findings.title: Tendon and Ligament Repair
findings.content:
Some of the most robust data comes from tendon injury models. A study published in the Journal of Applied Physiology showed that BPC-157 dramatically improved healing of transected (cut) Achilles tendons in rats. Treated tendons exhibited better strength, structure, and cell survival with less inflammation.

Additional experiments demonstrated accelerated healing of damaged knee ligaments and increased outgrowth of tendon cells, suggesting the peptide can stimulate cells to rebuild connective tissue. Researchers observed that even without additional growth factors, BPC-157 alone enhanced tendon cell migration and viability at injury sites.

findings.title: Bone Healing
findings.content: A study in rabbits with non-healing bone defects found that local BPC-157 treatment was as effective as bone graft surgery in mending the defect. The peptide-treated rabbits showed new bone formation bridging the gap, similar to rabbits that received bone tissue transplants, suggesting BPC-157 may trigger regenerative processes in bone tissue.

findings.title: Gastric Protection
findings.content: BPC-157 was initially studied as a "cytoprotective" agent in the stomach, meaning it can protect stomach cells from injury. In rat studies, BPC-157 demonstrated the ability to prevent and heal stomach ulcers, including ulcers caused by NSAID painkillers, which are known for eroding the stomach lining. The peptide also protected the GI tract from alcohol-induced damage.

findings.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease Models
findings.content: Beyond the stomach, BPC-157 showed benefits in inflammatory bowel disease models. Rats with ulcerative colitis (a severe gut inflammation) recovered faster and had reduced intestinal damage when given BPC-157. A preliminary clinical trial in people with ulcerative colitis reported positive results, though full details have not been published.

findings.title: Anti-Inflammatory Effects
findings.content: In rat models of induced inflammatory arthritis, animals treated with BPC-157 had reduced joint swelling, less inflammatory cell buildup, and better preserved joint function than untreated rats. The peptide appeared to protect joints from autoimmune damage.

findings.title: Neuroprotection
findings.content: BPC-157 has shown promise as a neuroprotective compound in animal studies. It helped preserve brain cells in rodent experiments of traumatic brain injury and stroke, and produced antidepressant-like effects in a rat model of chronic stress. Rats with symptoms of depression or anxiety exhibited improved behaviors after BPC-157 treatment, correlating with modulation of serotonin and dopamine systems.

findings.title: Organ Protection
findings.content: In laboratory rodents, BPC-157 reduced damage to the liver caused by toxic chemicals and improved survival in cases of acute liver failure. Similarly, it lessened heart muscle damage in animal models of certain cardiac injuries, suggesting potential cardio-protective effects.

BPC-157 was originally discovered in human gastric juice during gastroenterology research. In simple terms, a peptide is a short chain of amino acids – the building blocks of proteins. This particular peptide has been nicknamed the "body protection compound" in research circles due to the broad protective effects observed on the body's tissues in laboratory studies.

Unlike many peptides that are quickly broken down by digestive enzymes, BPC-157 demonstrates exceptional stability. This characteristic means the peptide could potentially be administered orally and still exert effects, unlike most peptides that must be given by injection. In rodent studies, BPC-157 proved effective when administered through various routes including intramuscular and intravenous injection, demonstrating bioavailability and activity in the body.

It's important to clarify that BPC-157 is an experimental compound. It is not approved as a medication by regulatory agencies and is officially designated for research use only at present. Despite this regulatory status, interest in BPC-157 has grown substantially due to promising early research findings in preclinical models.

BPC-157 stands out as a compound at the frontier of medical research. From a research perspective, it demonstrates several noteworthy characteristics: it's small and stable, easy to administer in various forms, and has shown remarkable healing capabilities in preclinical models across the board – from mending torn tendons to healing ulcerated gastrointestinal tissues and protecting neural cells.

However, a key message is caution. As of now, BPC-157 is not an approved treatment for any condition and remains in the realm of experimental research. The peptide is currently available only as a research tool, and any human use is essentially an off-label experiment. While current findings in the laboratory are inspiring, science demands evidence through well-designed human studies.

The current state of knowledge presents a paradox: enthusiastic reports and underground usage suggest it may help people recover from injuries, yet solid clinical data to fully back up those claims and ensure long-term safety is lacking. Until comprehensive human studies are completed, experts advise that BPC-157 should be confined to laboratories and carefully controlled trials.

Researchers around the world are actively studying this peptide, as evidenced by increasing publications and even patents, because its multi-faceted actions are unlike anything in current therapeutic arsenals. For those learning about BPC-157, the best course is to stay informed but cautious. With time and rigorous research, we will discover whether BPC-157 can safely fulfill its healing reputation and possibly become a mainstream therapeutic agent. Until then, it remains a compelling scientific discovery on the path from laboratory to clinical application.

old_values:
TB-500 represents a unique approach to tissue repair research — one focused on cellular mobilization rather than direct growth factor stimulation. Its mechanism of action through actin dynamics provides a complementary pathway to other repair peptides, which is why it has become one of the most commonly combined compounds in multi-peptide research protocols.

The preclinical evidence base is substantial, particularly for cardiac repair, wound healing, and neuroinflammation. Clinical investigation of the parent compound Thymosin Beta-4 has progressed furthest in ophthalmology, with Phase 2/3 trials for corneal healing providing the strongest clinical validation of the biological mechanism.

For researchers, TB-500 offers a well-characterized compound with a clear mechanistic profile and extensive preclinical support. Its complementary mechanism to BPC-157 — systemic cell migration versus localized growth factor signaling — explains why the two compounds are so frequently studied together.

As with all research peptides, TB-500 is designated for research use only and is not approved for human therapeutic use. Researchers should source from vendors with third-party COA documentation and verified purity testing.
